questions.q: Peak is 10,000 rps and one app server handles 1,000 rps. You size for ρ ≈ 0.6 at peak. About how many servers?
questions.why: Replicas = peak ÷ (capacity × 0.6) = 10,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 16.7. 10 is ρ = 1.0 (backs up), 11 is ρ ≈ 0.9 (no room for a spike or a dead server).
questions.note: Capacity cheat sheet: what one box handles

questions.q: 10,000 rps arrive at 2 service replicas that handle 1,000 rps each. What is ρ?
questions.why: ρ = arriving ÷ capacity = 10,000 ÷ 2,000 = 5. Anything at or above 1 means the queue grows and requests drop.

questions.q: A server handles 1,000 rps and each request takes 20 ms. How many requests are in flight at once (Little's law)?
questions.why: In flight = throughput × time = 1,000/s × 0.020 s = 20. The sim treats such a replica as 20 workers sharing one line.
questions.note: M/M/c: how the wait is calculated

questions.q: Two coffee shops are both 90% busy. Shop A has 1 barista; Shop B has 10 baristas and one shared line. Who waits less, and why?
choices: Shop A, because one line is simpler
The same, because both are 90% busy
Shop B, because you only wait if all ten baristas are busy at once
Shop B, because each barista works faster
questions.why: Same utilization, but with random arrivals one of ten is usually free. At 90%: ~18 min wait with 1 barista vs ~1.3 min with 10 (2-minute drinks).
questions.note: M/M/c in plain words: the coffee shop

questions.q: With ONE worker, how much longer is the average queue wait at ρ = 0.9 than at ρ = 0.5?
questions.why: One worker: wait ∝ ρ ÷ (1 − ρ). 0.9 ÷ 0.1 = 9 vs 0.5 ÷ 0.5 = 1, so 9×. A box with many workers stays near zero much longer, then climbs.
questions.note: Capacity cheat sheet: what one box handles

questions.q: In an M/M/1 queue (one worker), the chance a new request has to wait equals…
questions.why: With one worker you wait exactly when it's busy, and it's busy a fraction ρ of the time. With c workers that chance is Erlang C, which is much smaller.
questions.note: M/M/c: how the wait is calculated

questions.q: Ten baristas, ten separate lines (one each), same total load. Compared with one shared line, waits are…
choices: Longer: it behaves like ten 1-barista shops
questions.why: You can be stuck behind a slow order while the next barista is idle. That's why a load balancer that picks a free server beats random assignment.
questions.note: M/M/c in plain words: the coffee shop

questions.q: A service sends 5,000,000 bytes per second. That's…
questions.why: 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes, so 5,000,000 bytes/s = 5 MB/s. Unit slips like 5,000 MB/s are a classic estimation mistake.
